name: The Game of Chicken
statement: Two players race toward a collision; each wants the other to swerve, and mutual nerve is the worst outcome for both.
statementAccent: each wants the other to swerve
meaning: The game of chicken is an anti-coordination game modelling two players on a collision course. In the classic image, two drivers speed toward each other and each can swerve or go straight. If both go straight they crash, the worst outcome for both; if both swerve, they tie, each surviving but winning nothing; if one swerves while the other goes straight, the one who held his nerve wins and the swerver loses face. The defining tension is that each player would rather go straight if the other swerves, but rather swerve if the other goes straight.
mechanism: Because each player's best move depends on the other's, the game has no dominant strategy. Swerving is the best response to Straight, and going straight is the best response to Swerve, which gives two pure-strategy equilibria, the asymmetric outcomes in which one yields and the other does not, plus a mixed equilibrium in which each randomises. The instability of who yields is the heart of the game. A player can win by making his commitment to go straight credible and irreversible, so the other, seeing that yielding is impossible for him, is compelled to swerve.

examples.text: Two drivers speed head-on and the first to swerve is the 'chicken', the everyday image from which the game takes its name.

Schelling's insight: a driver who conspicuously and irreversibly disables his own steering, visibly removing his option to swerve, forces the other to yield, since the commitment is credible only because it is observable and cannot be undone.
The Cuban Missile Crisis is routinely analysed as chicken, two powers pushing a dangerous situation toward the edge of catastrophe, each hoping the other backs down first.

variants.name: Hawk-dove
variants.text: The evolutionary form introduced by Maynard Smith and Price in 1973, formally identical to chicken when the cost of fighting exceeds the value of the contested resource, and foundational to the idea of an evolutionarily stable strategy.

variants.name: The rationality of irrationality
variants.text: Schelling's point that appearing reckless, unpredictable, or unable to back down can be an advantage, because it makes the threat to go straight credible.

whyItMatters: It is a canonical model across game theory, international relations, and evolutionary biology, giving a precise structure to standoffs and brinkmanship. It illuminates nuclear confrontations, labour disputes and strikes, price wars, and political showdowns such as debt-ceiling and shutdown confrontations, and through its equivalence to hawk-dove it models evolutionary conflict over shareable resources. Above all it shows how a credible, irreversible commitment, even one that looks like folly, can determine who prevails.

working.text: expect the stable outcomes to be the two asymmetric ones in which one side yields, with no dominant strategy for either player.
recognise that visibly and irreversibly removing your own option to back down can force the other side to yield.
treat the both-go-straight outcome as catastrophic for both, the feature that distinguishes chicken from other conflict games.

limits: It is a highly simplified two-by-two model, while real standoffs involve incomplete information, many players, and repeated or dynamic play. Its predictions are also fragile: with two pure equilibria plus a mixed one and no dominant strategy, the theory does not single out a unique outcome, which is the source of the game's instability rather than a defect to be repaired. And the commitment strategies that win it depend on the commitment being genuinely observable and irreversible, conditions that are hard to meet and easy to bluff, so applying the model to real conflicts requires care.
misreadings: It is not the same as the prisoner's dilemma. In chicken, mutual defection, both going straight, is the worst outcome for both, whereas in the prisoner's dilemma mutual defection is bad but not the worst, and being the lone cooperator is worst. Consequently chicken has no dominant strategy, while in the prisoner's dilemma defection strictly dominates. It also has no single solution: there are two pure equilibria and a mixed one, not one predicted outcome. And the cliff-edge race in 'Rebel Without a Cause' is a variant, not the head-on form.
origin: The name comes from the mid-twentieth-century driving dare; Bertrand Russell drew the analogy to nuclear brinkmanship in 'Common Sense and Nuclear Warfare' (1959), Anatol Rapoport and Albert Chammah gave it formal treatment in 1966, and it is equivalent to the hawk-dove game of Maynard Smith and Price (1973).
